descs.en: A garden that only exists at midnight. Flowers that archive grief. A keeper who must learn to let things go.

chapters.desc: She tends flowers that should not exist.
chapters.title: The Garden That Blooms at the End of the World
chapters.content:
The garden existed in the hour between midnight and one, and only Mei Ruolan could find it.

She had discovered it the winter she turned nineteen, following a scent she could not name. Something like jasmine, or rain, or the silence a room keeps after someone leaves. She had pushed through a gap in a stone wall behind the old pharmacy and found: flowers. Dozens of them. Some had been extinct for a century. Some had never been catalogued. Some, as far as she could tell, had only ever existed in paintings.

She never decided to become its keeper. It happened one midnight at a time, until she could not imagine staying away.

✦   ✦   ✦

The first time Xiao Shang appeared, he was sitting on a stone bench in the middle of the night garden eating a tangerine with an air of complete ownership.

"You're trespassing," said Mei Ruolan.

"We're both trespassing," he said. "This garden belongs to someone who hasn't been born yet." He peeled another segment. "I've been waiting for you to find it. You took longer than expected."

"Who are you?"

He looked at her as if he had known her for a very long time, and spent most of it waiting.

"That," he said, "is the question the garden brought you here to answer."
chapters.epigraph: "Every impossible thing begins as someone's refusal to accept the possible."

chapters.desc: Plants that remember. A boy who sees tomorrow.
chapters.title: What Flowers Know
chapters.content:
The flowers in the midnight garden were not merely decorative. Mei Ruolan understood this in her second month as keeper, when the black iris in the eastern corner began to hum.

It was not a mechanical sound. It sounded like something remembering: low, rhythmic, in a key that matched no instrument she knew. She pressed her ear to the soil beside its roots and heard, or felt, the vibration of very old grief.

"The flowers are archives," Xiao Shang told her. He had taken to appearing without announcement at hours she could not predict, and she had taken to no longer being surprised by this. "Every feeling a person has suppressed long enough passes into the ground and eventually into a root." He crouched beside the iris. "This one has been holding someone's sorrow for approximately sixty years."

✦   ✦   ✦

"Can it be released?" she asked.

"That's why you're here," he said simply.

She looked at him. "You keep saying I was brought here for a reason. But you won't tell me what the reason is."

"Because," he said, and for the first time she heard something under his composure, something he had clearly been holding on to for a long time — "if I tell you the ending, you might not take the steps that lead to it." He stood. "And I have worked very hard to make sure you get there."
chapters.epigraph: "The root does not know the flower. The flower does not know the fruit. And yet they are the same continuous thing."

chapters.desc: Some endings are also beginnings. Some losses are also gifts.
chapters.title: The Last Bloom
chapters.content:
The garden bloomed one final time on the night of the winter solstice, and every flower in it opened at once. That did not happen in nature, or even in magic. It happened that night.

Mei Ruolan stood in the center of it and felt the accumulated grief of sixty years move through her like a tide going out — not painless, but purposeful. She understood, standing there, that she had been carrying something she never chose.

Xiao Shang stood at the edge of the garden. She looked at him across the blooming and the light.

✦   ✦   ✦

"You're leaving," she said. It was not a question.

"The garden's work is done," he said. "The grief has gone where it needed to go." He paused. "I was only ever here to bring you to the moment where you could do what you were meant to do."

"And what was that?"

He smiled. It was the first time, she realized, that she had seen him smile without the weight of knowing behind it. Just a smile. Just a person, briefly, in a garden at the end of a winter, glad.

"You let things be held," he said. "You let old sorrow become something that could finally breathe." He stepped back toward the gap in the wall. "Almost no one can do that." He paused again. "The garden will be here. It will have a new keeper. But it will remember you."

She watched him go. The flowers held their light a little longer, and then, one by one, slowly, as if they knew they were finished, they closed.
